26	- **Dirty.** A preset is dirty when it has unsaved edits.
27	- **Eval.** An automated test that gives a model a task and checks the transcript that results.
28	- **M0 to M5.** The milestones in which the tool catalog was delivered.
29	
30	## Current connection and execution boundary
31	
32	- The server starts automatically with the JusPrin Agent panel. There is no `JUSPRIN_MCP` switch to enable it and no bearer token. The server listens only on the numeric loopback address. It prefers port 47301, and falls back to a port chosen by the operating system only when 47301 is taken.
33	- The shell tells the server where its discovery file is: `<data_dir>/jusprin/mcp.json`. The running server writes its details there in one atomic step: the actual address, the PID, a unique `instanceId` for this run, the build version, and the protocol versions. Before a server removes the record, it checks, while holding the discovery lock, that the record is its own. An older server therefore cannot remove a newer server's record, even inside the same process. On POSIX systems the file has mode `0600`.
34	- The helper checks that the discovery file is valid, and then tests that the address in it answers. When the app starts or restarts later, the helper follows the new record. The helper never launches JusPrin. The discovery file holds one record, and the last server to write it wins. So the helper works with one selected instance; there is no way to choose among several. `--discovery`, `JUSPRIN_MCP_DISCOVERY`, and `JUSPRIN_MCP_URL` override the file path or the address. They do not switch anything on. The connection entries that Connect writes use `--discovery` with the app's actual data directory.
35	- When the app is not running, the helper answers discovery and tool-list requests from the registry compiled into the helper. Tool calls made while the app is not running return `workspace_unavailable`. When the app can be reached, the helper uses the app's live catalog and results, even when the app and the helper are different versions. Do not replace a live app's tool list with the helper's compiled one. A version difference between the two is logged.
36	- The HTTP adapter accepts MCP protocol version `2026-07-28`. The helper can also negotiate the older versions `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25`. The helper does all conversion between versions. Code that executes a tool must not behave differently for different protocol versions.
37	- **Connect** shows the person the command or the file edit and asks for confirmation first. Then it either runs the Claude Code or Codex CLI, or merges the JusPrin entry into the JSON configuration of Claude Desktop/local Cowork, Cursor or VS Code. A JSON edit keeps unrelated settings and makes a backup. It is refused when the preview is out of date or when the destination is a symlink. It does not protect against another editor writing the same file at the exact moment of replacement.
38	- On macOS the helper is bundled next to the app executable. Windows has a matching install rule. On Linux, the entry for an AppImage uses the installed image's path plus `--mcp-bridge`, and the app handles that flag before the GUI starts. Do not save a temporary AppImage mount path as the command.
39	
40	Workspace commands run on the GUI thread, through the shared coordinator. A timer owned by the shell keeps execution moving, so execution does not depend on the WebView's handshake. No external client ever gets direct access to OrcaSlicer objects.
41	
42	A call from an external client is tagged `ToolSource::Mcp`. The MCP adapter sets that tag, so it can be trusted, and it is kept for the activity history and for diagnostics. External calls run through the same coordinator and the same workspace commands as calls from the in-app Agent. The change log records the edits they make, as it records every edit, and marks them `external`. In the conversation thread those edits appear as rows that say "External tool", where a change made in the app says "Agent".
43	
44	## Start with an eval failure
45	
46	The fact that OrcaSlicer has a menu item or a config key is not a reason to add a tool. Start from a transcript or an automated eval in which the Agent cannot finish a real user task, finishes it only some of the time, or needs an unreasonable number of steps or tokens.
47	
48	Write down:
49	
50	- what the user wanted to achieve;
51	- the exact point where the current tools stop being enough;
52	- which OrcaSlicer state or operation is missing;
53	- what a successful transcript should look like;
54	- the unsafe or ambiguous cases that must fail; and
55	- the evidence that will show the new tool fixed the problem.
56	
57	If the failure can be fixed by a clearer description, a better result, or a more useful validation error, improve the existing definition instead of adding a tool.
58	
59	The candidate catalog later in this guide lists tools we might build. Being listed there does not accept a tool, and it does not excuse a tool from this section. A row in that catalog does two jobs. It records which product screen and which group of evals the tool would serve, which makes the eval easier to write. It also settles what the tool acts on, its action class, and its OrcaSlicer owner, so that two people do not build the same capability twice under different names.
60	
61	## Decide whether this should be a tool
62	
63	Add or extend a tool when the Agent needs one of three things: up-to-date state read straight from OrcaSlicer, a calculation that OrcaSlicer does and that always gives the same answer for the same input, or a change to the live project.
64	
65	Do not add a tool for:
66	
67	- a single setting key. Setting keys are records that the generic settings tools search and edit;
68	- general printing advice that the model can work out from a skill;
69	- a fixed bundle of changes such as "make it stronger", where the right answer depends on the part and on what the user cares about;
70	- driving the UI, such as pressing a button or operating a widget or a hidden panel;
71	- data that an existing tool already returns in a size-limited result;
72	- a capability someone might want in the future, with no eval or user task behind it; or
73	- an operation that the real workspace adapter cannot truly perform through the OrcaSlicer class that owns it.
74	
75	A fixed, mechanical step of a workflow can be a tool. Examples are generating OrcaSlicer's calibration geometry and starting OrcaSlicer's slice action. Advice should stay a skill until there is a separately specified operation behind it that always behaves the same way.
76	
77	## Skills versus tools
78	
79	A skill is text the model reads. A tool is something the app executes. To decide which one a candidate is, ask one question: does it have to run, or does it only have to be read?
80	
81	- It has to run if it reads state the model does not have, computes something only OrcaSlicer can compute, or changes the project. That makes it a tool.
82	- It only has to be read if it is judgement, the order to do things in, facts about printing, how to interpret a tool's result, or which question to ask first. That makes it a skill.
83	
84	The section above covers tools. This section covers skills, and decides the cases that fall in between.
85	
86	A skill contains things the model could do by itself if it had the right knowledge. It contains nothing that executes. Examples:
87	
88	- judging evidence, such as telling an adhesion failure from wet filament in a photo;
89	- the order of a series of tool calls, and the reasons for that order. For "make it stronger": read the settings, change walls and infill, slice, read the report;
90	- facts about printing, such as what PETG tolerates;
91	- which question to ask when the answer would change the plan.
92	
93	A skill is a file on the Agent page, `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: frontmatter with its `name` and a `trigger`, a `description` or both, then the text the model gets. The page sends every skill once per connection with the `skills` bridge message. A skill with a trigger is the app's: when the event it names happens, the host adds it to the one request where the model first reads about the event, as the request's last item, and to no later request. A skill with a description is the model's: `skill_read` lists the described skills in its own description and returns one by name, and is offered only while at least one exists (none does yet). Four skills have triggers, one file each:
94	
95	- `file-loaded` (trigger `file_loaded`): the first message after a file is opened or imported is a judgement about the load report. It fires when the person opens or drops a file, after an in-app `object_import` (and a failed `project_open`) in the same turn, and in the opened project's chat after an in-app `project_open`, which replaces the conversation and so ends the turn that asked. An MCP client's loads fire nothing. The host sends a picture of the active plate with it and, when no purpose is recorded, one sentence of its own built from that state.
96	- `project-setup-changed` (trigger `setup_changed`): check the setup in force against the print's purpose. It fires on the result of an in-app `setup_record` that recorded a purpose for the first time or changed its fields (its result says which in `purposeChange`; a call that only restates the title to change the plan does not fire it), when the printer, filament, process or plate type differs from the setup the model was last asked to check under a recorded purpose (on the next tool result of the turn, or on the next turn's first request when the person changed it by hand), and on a turn's first request after the person restored an earlier version while a purpose is recorded. Each time the model is asked to check, the app saves the setup in force as the one checked. The model's own successful `printer_setup` fires nothing: the setup it chose is saved as checked at once (Kenneth, 2026-10-19), so the skill is for a setup that moved without the model, and a pairing its change breaks is caught by the slice-refusal facts and skill. It gives way to the file-loaded skill on a request that carries both, since that skill already asks for the same check.
97	- `slice-failed` (trigger `slice_failed`): a plate's last slice did not succeed, because OrcaSlicer's check refused the plate or the run failed. The adapter records why on the plate (`WorkspacePlate::slice_failure`: refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the setting and object when named) at the moment it happens (a hook in `Plater::reslice`, `Workspace/SliceRequests.hpp`, and the run's completion event), worded by the print-issue monitor's `slice_failure_of`, and keeps it until the plate slices. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceFailure`; `slice_report` of an unsliced plate adds the check code and the object's name. The skill fires once per failure, on the first request that carries it: the result of the model's own `slice_start`, the turn the app starts when a slice the model started fails after its turn, or the next message after the person's Slice all. The same refusal again is the same failure.
98	- `print-issues` (trigger `print_issues`): what the print-issue chip's two buttons ask for and how to read what OrcaSlicer reports. The adapter reads a slice's warnings through the monitor's `slice_warnings_of` while the plate is active and keeps a summary on the plate while that slice is current (`WorkspacePlate::slice_warnings`: the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning, critical first, in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object). It counts every warning the chip lists, so the bed-temperature warning too, which `slice_report` leaves out. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceWarnings`. The skill fires on the request that carries a chip's message, and on the first request whose workspace shows warnings no request has carried yet, whether the person sliced (their next message) or the model did (the tool result that shows them, or the app's turn when its slice ended after its turn); a re-slice with the same warnings fires nothing.
99	
100	The cases in between:
101	
102	- **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).
103	- **An analysis.** It is a tool when OrcaSlicer computes it and always gets the same answer, such as overhang angles from geometry. It is a skill when it is a judgement about evidence. Pair that skill with the tool that supplies the evidence (`view_render`, `slice_report`).
104	- **Large reference data.** When the model needs only one part of the data, make it a tool that returns the part an argument selects, as `settings_search` does. When the model needs to see all of the data before it can use any of it, make it text. The printer list described under [Input design](#input-design) is the case we measured: putting the whole list in the instructions worked better than the search tool.
105	- **A tool description versus a skill.** A tool description says when to call that one tool, in the words a person would use. A skill says how several tools fit together and what to conclude from their results. If a tool description has grown into a step-by-step procedure, move the procedure out into a skill.
106	
107	When you are not sure, start with a skill. A skill is a text file that ships with the page. A tool costs the whole implementation sequence described below, including fakes, tests, and rebase evidence. Turn a skill into a tool only on the kind of evidence every tool starts from (see [Start with an eval failure](#start-with-an-eval-failure)). Either transcripts show the model getting the sequence wrong in ways that better text does not fix, or the action needs something only the app can give: all-or-nothing application, validation, or undo. The opposite sign exists too. If a skill has turned into exact values and calls in a fixed order, with no judgement between them, it should be written as a tool.
108	
109	How something gets loaded into the model's context does not decide whether it is a skill or a tool. Today a skill costs its one line in the instructions, and a tool costs its definition on the first request of a conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). If we later use the model platform's deferred loading, both will cost one index line plus a load when needed. A skill could then be a deferred read-only tool: the tool's description is the skill's index line, and the tool's result is the skill's text. Tools and skills would then be found the same way and covered by the same eval.
110	
111	## Read, mutation, and destructive policy
112	
113	Decide what a tool may do from its action class in the registry, not from its name:
114	
115	- **Read-only:** cannot change the project, a preset, anything on disk, the printer, or any product state that is saved.
116	- **Mutation:** changes the project, a preset, or saved product state.
117	- **Destructive:** may delete, overwrite, discard, print, export, or restore history.
118	
119	The action class is information used for UI wording, MCP annotations, staleness checks, and the audit history. A valid tool call starts as soon as it has been validated. A tool that previews changes counts as read-only only if tests against both the fake and the real workspace adapter prove that it does none of these: make a preset dirty, raise the workspace revision, create history, cancel slicing, or write a file.
120	
121	## Asynchronous operations
122	
123	Make a tool asynchronous only when the real OrcaSlicer operation is asynchronous. Do not build a second engine for running jobs.
124	
125	Slicing, and any long-running action added later, works like this:
126	
127	1. The workspace command starts the work through its current OrcaSlicer owner and returns a stable action handle.
128	2. `ToolActivity` records that the action is running, and then its final state, with a limited amount of progress information.
129	3. When OrcaSlicer completes or fails, the workspace state advances or is invalidated.
130	4. After that event, the caller fetches the real slice report or the error.
131	5. Cancelling calls OrcaSlicer's real cancellation path, and reports whether the cancellation took effect before the work finished.
132	
133	MCP progress notifications are optional. They belong to one request and exist only to show progress. The progress value must never go backwards, and a client must always have another way to learn the final result. Add the MCP Tasks extension only when a real client or eval needs durable calls that outlive one request. An operation taking several seconds is not enough reason.
134	
135	The current coordinator runs an action in steps, on GUI ticks. It does not provide durable asynchronous jobs. The bridge accepts `notifications/cancelled` in both the legacy and the modern protocol versions. On receiving one, it closes the connection it was forwarding and suppresses any further output for that request. End of input (EOF) ends the bridge session. If the connection is lost before the final response, the client gets `connection_lost` with an **unknown outcome** warning. That is not proof that the mutation was cancelled. Never retry a mutation automatically after such a loss. Read the real state first.
136	
137	## Tool exposure
138	
139	By default, offer a tool through both adapters when both can supply the same inputs. Offer it through only one when the two sides get their context in different ways. The current cases:
140	
141	- `workspace_inspect` is offered through both adapters. Either side can then get the identity of a newly completed slice after slicing, without relying on the context it was given at the start of the turn.
142	- Import from an attachment (`object_import`) is in-app only, and import from a path (`object_import_file`) is MCP only. In the first case the file reaches the app through the conversation. In the second it arrives as an explicit path. These are two separate definitions that each say exactly what they do, both built on one workspace command. They are not one tool that behaves differently for different callers.
143	- `setup_record` is in-app only. The intent record and the pinned plan belong to the in-app chat. An external agent keeps what its user said, and its own plan, in its own conversation. MCP clients can still read both through `workspace_inspect` and `slice_report`. For the same reason, the in-app assistant's print guidance, which names these tools, is not part of the MCP server's instructions. That guidance is the "Intent and setup", "Preparation" and "Verification" paragraphs of the in-app prompt, written on the page in `AgentUI/src/projectInstructions.ts`.
144	- A future MCP diagnostics tool may be MCP only, if its purpose is to establish the external connection.
145	- The printer panel's five own tools carry only the `Printer` exposure. Neither adapter lists them. The panel's conversation offers all of them in every mode and refuses the calls that do not fit the conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). What the model reads back from one of these tools is the tool's own result. It is not wrapped in the host's workspace envelope.
146	
147	Write the reason for a restricted exposure next to the registry definition, and test it. Do not use exposure to make one tool behave differently for different callers. If two adapters need different behavior, either improve the shared command or create two separate definitions that each say what they really do.
148	
149	## When resources or skills are appropriate
150	
151	Do not make anything depend on MCP resources until the clients we intend to support have shown that their models fetch resources reliably. A tool that returns a size-limited amount of data is what every client can be expected to handle. Resources may be added as an optional second way to get data that is large, readable, and stable.
152	
153	Keep printing playbooks as skills the model can read (see [Skills versus tools](#skills-versus-tools)). Examples are reducing stringing, improving strength, and choosing a support strategy. Turn a workflow into an executable tool only when it corresponds to a named OrcaSlicer operation that always behaves the same way and has defined inputs, outputs, validation, and behavior for undo, reset, and cancellation. If many step-by-step workflows eventually qualify, build one workflow registry that the model can search, in preference to dozens of nearly identical tool definitions.
154	
155	## Required implementation sequence for one new tool
156	
157	1. Add or update the failing eval and the expected transcript.
158	2. Find the real OrcaSlicer owner. Record how it behaves: object lifetimes, threading, undo history, and events.
159	3. Define the typed inputs, outputs, and errors of the workspace command.
160	4. Implement the command in the fake workspace adapter, and write the workspace contract tests.
161	5. Implement the command in the real workspace adapter, through the smallest possible seam in the owner.
162	6. Prove that making the edit directly in the GUI and making it through the tool leave the same observable state.
163	7. Add the registry definition, the decoder and validator, the link to the code that executes the tool, and the output schema.
164	8. Add coordinator tests for action class, staleness, all-or-nothing behavior, cancellation, and the final activity state.
165	9. Add projection tests for every adapter that offers the tool.
166	10. Add protocol fixtures and output-limit tests.
167	11. Run a harness against the real app, and record one end-to-end transcript with an external client.
168	12. Update the catalog below, and attach the verification and rebase evidence to the PR.
169	
170	Do not merge a registry entry that is backed only by the fake workspace.
171	
172	## Test matrix
173	
174	Every new capability needs tests at each layer it passes through:
175	
176	| Layer | Evidence |
177	|---|---|
178	| Registry | unique name, deterministic ordering, valid schemas, correct exposure and action class |
179	| Decoder | valid inputs, unknown fields, type errors, bounds, conflicting selectors |
180	| Fake workspace | success, expected failures, revision, events, atomicity, native undo/reset/revert and cancel semantics |
181	| Coordinator | stale session/revision, cancellation race, terminal result |
182	| Real adapter | live Orca owner, GUI parity, truthful undo/reset/revert behavior, slicing invalidation/completion, document replacement |
183	| OpenAI adapter | canonical schema projection and successful continuation |
184	| MCP adapter | canonical schema/output projection, bounded response, protocol errors, disconnect behavior |
185	| Shell/eval | real project and intended client complete the user task |
186	
187	If a layer does not apply, say why in the PR. If something cannot be tested, state that openly as a limitation. It is not permission to leave out evidence without saying so.

263	
264	These will not be tools:
265

275	### Prerequisites the catalog imposes on the machinery
276	
277	The catalog needs the following to be in place:
278	
279	- `validate_output` supports `enum` (used for provenance, action state, region kind, and section names) and `maxLength`, so a row may use them. Inputs that allow several alternative forms, such as the facets of `object_place`, are checked by the decoder, not by the schema validator.
280	- Neither adapter needs new code for loading tools. The projection tests need to record definition bytes for each adapter, and the live regression test needs to record input and cached tokens for each request. With those numbers the deferral decision can rest on evidence.

282	  - the mapping and readiness logic in `SelectMachineDialog`, needed by `preflight_check`;

result.output:
## 2.11 Calibration and troubleshooting

This surface answers: **Is the printer-material combination behaving as expected?**

The audit found both guided calibration pages and more advanced generators.

### Relevant calibration capabilities

- Flow dynamics
- Flow rate
- Temperature
- Pressure advance
- Retraction
- Maximum volumetric speed
- VFA
- Junction deviation
- Input-shaping frequency and damping

### Why the agent cannot completely own calibration

Calibration depends on physical evidence:

- Filament may be wet.
- Adhesion may be poor.
- Transparent or reflective filament may confuse optical sensors.
- A nozzle may be worn or partially obstructed.
- A user may judge two samples differently.
- Automatic measurements contain uncertainty.
- An apparently better surface may reduce strength or accuracy elsewhere.

### What the agent should do

The agent should:

1. Diagnose the observed symptom.
2. Decide whether calibration is justified.
3. Select the appropriate test.
4. Choose safe test ranges.
5. Explain what to observe.
6. Analyze sensor data or photographs.
7. Recommend a result.
8. Say what was saved to the printer or filament profile and that it can be changed back.

The user should not be presented with every calibration parameter unless manual control is requested.

---

## 2.12 Privacy, updates, portability, and expert administration
## Writing UI code

Rules for anyone, human or agent, adding or changing a JusPrin surface. They
exist because every value that is typed by hand drifts from the design system and
from the other side of the app within weeks; today's guards catch most of it, but
only if the code goes through the token file in the first place.

1. **Never type a color, radius, font, or control size.** Every one comes
   from `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`. Native code reads it
   through `ShellTheme`: `palette(dark)` for color, `metrics()` for radii,
   spacing, and per-component sizes, `font(role)` for type. A stock
   `wxStaticText`, `wxTextCtrl`, or OrcaSlicer `Button` is
   dressed through `Shell/ShellRecipes.hpp`, never by calling its setters
   with literals. The Agent page uses only `var(--…)`: `--<group>-<name>` for
   color, `--radius-<name>`, `--font-<role>`, `--font-code`, and
   `--button-<recipe>-padding`.
2. **If the value you need has no token, add the token first.** Put it in
   the JSON, extend the guard in `tests/brand/test_brand_tokens.cpp` so a
   later edit cannot silently move it, then read it from code. Do not write
   the number "for now": the guards cannot see a literal that is already
   there, and the next reader cannot tell a decision from an accident. A
   value that exists in the design artifacts but not in the roles or scales is a design
   decision to raise, not a reason to type it.
3. **Layout spacing may stay literal, on the scale.** Padding between
   regions, gaps, and margins use 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, or 48 DIP.
   Control padding is not layout spacing; it comes from a button recipe.
4. **Pick the nearest role, never a bespoke size.** The roles are the whole
   type system. Bold at a body or label size is a role of its own; if a
   surface seems to need a size that no role has, see rule 2.
5. **The design system wins when it and the code disagree.** The two Claude
   artifacts are the source of truth (Kenneth, 2026-10-20; Figma is
   retired): the Design System
   (https://claude.ai/artifact/3zgiix8rAw3rXextQnR5UL) and the "JusPrin v2"
   canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v). Change the
   token file to match, or, when the code's value is the one to keep, change
   the artifact first. Do not trust old commit messages about either.
6. **Run the guards before calling UI work done:** `brand_tokens_tests`,
   `shell_theme_tests`, and `npm test` in `AgentUI`. Then look at the surface
   in the running app; the guards prove the code went through the tokens,
   not that the result looks right.
7. **Upstream files are off limits for style.** OrcaSlicer's own screens are
   retinted through the hooks `BrandPalette.cpp` installs and nothing else;
   see [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md). Their radii and fonts stay
   OrcaSlicer's until the surface is replaced.

content.text:
The usage limit was reached, so I stopped partway through step 1. The code for step 1 (the `calibration_generate` tool) is written. The checks against real OrcaSlicer have not run yet, so I'm not reporting step 1 as passing.

**Where the work is:** worktree `C:\src\JusPrin\.claude\worktrees\calibration`, branch `claude/calibration`, rebased onto `f323db81c7`. It's one temporary commit, "WIP calibration (temporary)", which should be rewritten into a real commit once the tests pass. The main checkout was not touched.

**What's built:**
- **The tool.** A registry entry, in-app only, classed as a mutation. A range that OrcaSlicer's own dialog would refuse is refused before anything closes.
- **How it runs.** It saves and releases the open project through the same path `project_open` uses (now one shared helper), then calls Orca's generator. The generator's own `new_project` then only replaces an empty project, so nothing asks a question. This is option one of handoff 5.1, with no "project is fresh" seam.
- **What it reports.** What Orca actually made, read back from Orca: the plate, the objects and the range applied. It also gives a one-sentence summary. The new test project's chat opens with that sentence as an app note, and the Agent's first turn starts there.
- **One upstream seam.** A public `Plater::set_project_name` beside `get_project_name`, needed for `projectName`. Merged against upstream `1bc39fd358`, both hunks land outside any conflict, and upstream has no such setter.

**Something the handoff didn't foresee:** saving a result as a calibrated copy would also save the test's own temporary edits to the filament. For example, the pressure-advance tower sets `slow_down_layer_time` to 1 s. The settings preview already warned about this but named only the setting, not its value. It now also gives each saved value, so the copy can keep them. The skill will need a line telling the agent to do that.

**Tests so far:**
- **Agent bridge tests (GUI-free):** all pass except one attachment-preview check. That check was added on 2026-10-20 and writes its fixture file in text mode, so on Windows it gets `\r\n` and fails. It isn't related to this work.
- **Written but not yet run:**
  - Catch2 checks in `tests/workspace` for the dialog rules.
  - Real-adapter harness checks for each of the three tests:
    - the project is saved with its unsaved edit first;
    - no empty project gets saved;

  - Seam (b) measurement by slicing: what a reopened test slices as, and whether setting the parameters again after the reopen brings the temperature range back.
  - Persist-as checks: read-only stock filament, saving the copy, and a second save updating it rather than making another.
- **Windows build fix:** since 2026-10-14 the adapter harness hasn't compiled on Windows, because `<windows.h>` turns a variable named `far` into nothing. I renamed it.

**Left to do:**
- Finish the background GUI build and set up software OpenGL for this build folder: `provision-mesa-windows.ps1 -BuildDir C:\b\cal`.
- Run the adapter harness and `workspace_contract_tests`, then turn the WIP commit into a real one.

Since your answers I've made three changes:
- **MCP:** `calibration_generate` is now offered to external MCP clients too. Only the in-app Agent also gets the opening note and first turn in the new test project's chat.
- **Seam (a):** each plate in the workspace now carries a `calibration` fact (test, start, end, step). It's read straight from Orca's per-layer state, so it's there while the test's steps are live and gone once Orca drops them, for example after a save and reopen. The calibration skill will use its absence to offer to regenerate.
- **Write in place or copy:** I'll put that in the skill as a question the agent asks the person.

The first harness run also found two real problems, both now fixed:
- **A stray empty project on Home.** Orca's generator starts with its own "new project" step. That made autosave keep the empty in-between project as a project of its own. JusPrin's release hook now skips that save while a test is being generated, which needs no change to Orca's code.
- **A wrong saved value in a preview warning.** The `saves_unsaved_edits` warning (new in this step) showed the edited value where it should show the saved one.

On seam (b), before removing it: re-applying the saved parameters after a reopen did bring the 230–250 °C range back. So (b) works mechanically, though you've chosen (a).

using System;
using System.Runtime.InteropServices;
public static class Win {
  [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential)] public struct RECT { public int Left, Top, Right, Bottom; }
  [DllImport("user32.dll")] public static extern bool GetWindowRect(IntPtr h, out RECT r);
  [DllImport("user32.dll")] public static extern bool SetForegroundWindow(IntPtr h);
  [DllImport("user32.dll")] public static extern bool SetProcessDPIAware();
}
"@
[Win]::SetProcessDPIAware() | Out-Null

[Win]::SetForegroundWindow($p.MainWindowHandle) | Out-Null
Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 400
$r = New-Object Win+RECT
[Win]::GetWindowRect($p.MainWindowHandle, [ref]$r) | Out-Null
$w = $r.Right - $r.Left; $h = $r.Bottom - $r.Top
$bmp = New-Object System.Drawing.Bitmap $w, $h
$g = [System.Drawing.Graphics]::FromImage($bmp)
$g.CopyFromScreen($r.Left, $r.Top, 0, 0, $bmp.Size)
$bmp.Save($Out, [System.Drawing.Imaging.ImageFormat]::Png)

content.text:
Yes, step 1 is now tested on the Windows VM, and the 12 screenshots are above. They are real captures of the app window, taken while the test harness ran each step. Everything for step 1 passes:
- **Real-app harness:** all 105 calibration checks pass. Its one failure is an older check whose expected wording doesn't match OrcaSlicer's Windows text.
- **Agent bridge tests:** 380 of 381. The one failure is a test from 2026-10-20 that breaks on Windows line endings.
- **Workspace contract tests:** all 44.

**What the screenshots show, for each test (flow, pressure advance, temperature):**
- **Before and after:** the person's project with an unsaved filament edit, then the test project that replaces it. The title shows the test's name and the plate holds Orca's test objects: 11 flow tiles, the pressure-advance tower, or the temperature tower labelled 230 to 250.
- **Pressure advance, sliced:** Preview coloured by pressure advance shows the tower rising from 0 to 0.1, as asked.
- **Temperature, sliced:** Preview coloured by temperature shows the tower stepping from 250 °C down to 230 °C.
- **Temperature, saved and reopened:** Preview is a single 250 °C. That is fact 2 of the handoff: the steps are not saved in the file. The workspace now reports this, which is the seam (a) you chose.
- **After saving a result:** the window once the result is saved as a calibrated copy of the filament.

**What the checks behind them confirm:**
- The person's project is saved to version history with their unsaved edit before the test project replaces it, and that edit is not carried into the test.

Add calibration_generate: one of OrcaSlicer's calibration tests as a project of its own

A calibration is a project of its own (Kenneth, 2026-10-21): OrcaSlicer's
generators call new_project() and edit the project-wide presets, so a test
cannot live on a plate of another project. calibration_generate makes a
temperature tower, the flow-ratio tiles or a pressure-advance test with the
parameters Orca's dialogs take, refusing what those dialogs refuse before
anything is closed. It is offered in-app and over MCP, as a mutation.

The open project is released through the path project_open uses, now one
helper (release_project): saved to its version history, unsaved preset edits
then dropped. The generator's own new_project then replaces an empty project.
Measured in the real app, that empty project was being saved as a managed
project of its own, so the shell's release hook now skips the save while the
workspace is inside a generator call. The result reports what Orca made, read
back from the plate's print (Plater::fff_print is not the plate's): the plate,
its objects and the range applied, plus a summary sentence. For the in-app
Agent the test's project opens its chat with that sentence as an app note and
a turn, as an Agent-opened project does with its load report.

The test's steps are runtime-only in Orca (a reopened tower slices at one
temperature). Each plate now reports them as a calibration fact while its
print holds them, for the calibration skill to read (seam (a), Kenneth's
choice; re-applying the parameters after a reload was measured to work too).

Saving a result as a calibrated copy would also save the test's own edits
(the pressure-advance tower sets slow_down_layer_time to 1 s). Preview's
saves_unsaved_edits warning now gives each edit's saved value, so the copy
can keep it.

Upstream footprint: a public Plater::set_project_name beside
get_project_name (Plater.hpp +1, Plater.cpp +5), for the caller's project
name; the generators name the project themselves. Neutral and additive;
no upstream line deleted or rewritten. Rebase simulation against
upstream/main 1bc39fd358 (merge base 8500fcdcca): Plater.hpp and
Plater.cpp already conflict at f323db81c7 for older fork seams; both new
hunks merge outside every conflict, and upstream has no such setter.

Tests: coordinator and Agent-host cases (agent_bridge_tests), the dialog
rules in workspace_contract_tests, and a real-adapter scenario in
workspace_adapter_integration_harness that generates each test from a
project with an unsaved edit, checks the version saved, the plate, the
print's parameters, the workspace fact and that one project exists per
test, slices the tower before and after a reopen, and saves results as
calibrated copies. JUSPRIN_CALIBRATION_CAPTURE=<folder> saves the window
at each step. The harness also builds on Windows again: a variable named
far is an empty macro there (336facf825).

Verified on Windows: all 105 calibration checks in the harness pass, as do
workspace_contract_tests; agent_bridge_tests passes except the
pick_attachment check that already fails on Windows (its fixture is
written in text mode), and the harness's slice_failure_in_orca_words
already fails there (Orca's Windows wording differs). Not run on macOS.

---
name: print-issues
trigger: print_issues
---

# Issues I report about the print

The rules above still apply. This request is the first to carry something I reported about the print: the person pressed a button on a print-issue chip (their message has a <print_issue> block), or a slice finished with warnings that plate's last slice did not have (the plate's sliceWarnings, in the workspace and in a tool result's slicing section; slice_report's findings section has the full list, except the heatbed warning and a repeated timelapse one).

The chip's buttons: "Explain this issue and my options." is a question, so answer it and leave the project as it is. "Help fix this issue." asks you to change what the issue names, and only that; anything else worth changing is a suggestion.

How to read a finding. A blocker means I will not slice or print until it is fixed; a warning means the slice exists and can print; a critical warning is one I flag as serious. The setting key names what to change, and settings_search or settings_get with that key tells what the setting is and its value now. The object, when named, narrows where; with none it is about the plate or the setup. count says how many warnings there are; read slice_report's findings when more than the first matters. An ignored one is a finding the person chose not to be told about again: still true of the slice. Explain a finding from its words, never from a cause you supply.

A warning is my statement about the slice, not proof the print will fail. Say what it risks for this print and its purpose. Some are the person's call because they trade the look, the time or their hardware: adding support (marks on the surface, clean-up), re-orienting, a filament pairing, a nozzle. A setting that only shapes the toolpath is yours to settle when the request covers it.

A finding counts as resolved only when a new slice no longer reports it, never because a setting changed or a chip was closed or ignored. Asked whether the print is ready, name what the slice still warns about.

| What I report while slicing | What it usually means, and where it points |
| --- | --- |
| "It seems object … has floating regions / floating cantilever / large overhangs. Please re-orient the object or enable support generation."; "Your model needs support!" | Parts start in the air or overhang far and will sag or fail without support. Support settings (enable_support, support_type) or orientation; which one is the person's call. |
| "Object can't be printed for empty layer between … and …" (critical) | Layers with nothing printed: features thinner than a line, or a broken mesh. object_analyze, object_repair, layer height or line widths. |
| "… is too close to others, and collisions may be caused."; "Prime Tower is too close to others"; "too close to exclusion area" | The nozzle or head may hit an object, the tower or a no-go area. Position (object_place, plate_layout) or print_sequence. |
| "Found gcode path conflicts between object … and …" (critical) | Two objects' paths cross. Spacing or layout. |
| "A G-code path goes beyond the plate boundaries." / "… beyond the max print height." | A skirt, brim, support or the object itself leaves the printable area by a little (more is a blocker). Position, brim_width, skirt_distance or size. |
| Speed, acceleration, jerk or junction deviation above the printer's maximum ("Orca will automatically cap …"); "Setting the jerk speed too low …" | It prints with the motion capped to the printer's limits. The setting named, or the printer's machine_max_* values. |
| A support base pattern replaced ("Rectilinear will be used instead") | I substitute a pattern this support type cannot use. support_base_pattern. |
| "Partial flushing volume set to 0 …"; "PLA and PETG filaments detected in the mixture …"; filament shrinkage or XY size compensation "will not be used"; different nozzle and filament diameters with the prime tower | Multi-filament settings: colours may mix, or a setting is dropped for this plate. Flushing volumes, the filaments chosen, the setting named. |
| "The current heatbed temperature is relatively high. The nozzle may clog when printing this filament in a closed environment. …" | The bed is at or above the filament's softening point; in a shut enclosure the heat can soften it before the nozzle. Opening the door or removing the top glass is the person's call; or lower this plate type's bed temperature. |
| "The nozzle hardness required by the filament is higher than …" | An abrasive filament wears the installed nozzle. Physical, the person's call: nozzle or filament. |
| Traditional timelapse "may cause surface imperfections"; smooth timelapse with the prime tower off | Only for a print that records a timelapse. timelapse_type, enable_prime_tower. |

I raise no slicing warning for thin walls, bridges, bed adhesion, brims or cooling. When the person asks about those, read slice_report's firstLayer, islands and supports sections and the settings; never present one as a warning I gave.
======
---
name: slice-failed
trigger: slice_failed
---

# A slice that did not succeed

The rules above still apply. A plate in the workspace now has a sliceFailure (slice_start's reason is the same record): its kind, my message, and the setting and objectId when I named them. It stays on the plate until the plate slices, so after a change it still shows the old reason until the next slice.

The kind says what happened. "refused": I checked the plate before slicing and started nothing, so there is no slice, no estimate and nothing to print, and slicing again unchanged is refused the same way. Change what the message names (a setting, or the filament and plate pairing), then slice again. "failed": the run started and stopped with an error partway; there is no usable slice either, and the message comes from the step that failed.

My check alone has about 150 distinct messages, many specific to a printer, a filament or a mode. Do not assume you know what one means beyond what it says, or why it happened. Read it this way: the setting key names what to change, and settings_search or settings_get with that key tells what the setting is and its value now; the object, when named, narrows where; with neither, it is about the plate or the setup as a whole. My message is the reason; do not add a different one. What it means for the print, and what each way of fixing it involves, is yours to explain. The check stops at the first problem it finds, so a slice after a fix may be refused for a different reason.

A problem counts as fixed only when a new slice no longer reports it. A change is a step towards that, not proof of it.

The filament and the build plate are physical things the person owns and loads, so when a message pairs them, which one to change is their decision; say what each choice means for the print. A setting that only shapes the toolpath (a layer height the nozzle can print, a support option, a line width) is yours to settle when the request covers it.

| Message family in my check | What it usually means |
| --- | --- |
| Layer height or a line width against the nozzle ("Layer height cannot exceed nozzle diameter", "Too large line width") | A process setting does not fit the selected nozzle; the setting key names which. |
| "Plate N: <plate type> is not suggested for use printing filament N (<filament>)" | That filament's preset has no bed temperature for this plate type; no setting is named. A different plate type or a different filament fixes it; the bed temperature the message offers instead prints a material on a surface its maker does not recommend. |
| An object that exceeds the build volume or its height, or collides with another when printed one by one | Size, position or print order; the object is named. Scaling changes the object the person wanted. |
| Organic or tree support diameters, support base patterns, support enforcers with support off | Support settings that contradict each other or are missing; the key names the one to change. |
| Prime tower requirements, an extruder the printer does not have, nozzles of different diameters | Multi-material or multi-extruder settings that disagree across objects or with the printer. |
| Spiral vase with more than one material, a smooth timelapse or clumping detection with the "by object" sequence | Two modes that cannot run together; one has to go, and which is the person's choice when it changes what they asked for. |
| Speed, acceleration or jerk above the printer's maximum; precise Z height or clumping detection beside the prime tower | Warnings, not refusals: I slice anyway, capping the motion values. |

---
name: calibration
description: Read when a print problem may come from the filament or its settings (stringing, under- or over-extrusion, gaps, bulging corners), when the person asks to calibrate a filament or printer, or when this project is a calibration test or they send a photo of one.
---

# Calibrating a filament on a printer

The rules above still apply. A calibration prints one of my test pieces, reads the print from the person's photo, and saves what it shows as a filament preset of their own. I have three tests: temperature, flow and pressure advance. Each one is a project of its own, made with calibration_generate.

## When a test is worth it

A test answers one question about this filament on this printer. Match it to what the person sees:

- Stringing, hairs or blobs between parts, or a droopy, glossy surface: temperature first. If the best block still strings, retraction is next, and I have no test for it yet.
- Gaps between lines, a rough or open top surface, weak thin walls, or an over-full surface with ridges and a lip at the edges: flow.
- Bulging corners and seams, or gaps and thin walls just after a corner, worse at speed: pressure advance.
- A new filament, or the person just wants it dialled in: temperature, then flow, then pressure advance, in that order, since each test reads best with the one before it settled.

Some problems come first, and a test would only measure them:

- Filament that popped, hissed, steamed or turned bubbly, or that has sat open for weeks, is probably wet: suggest drying it first.
- Extrusion that comes and goes, or under-extrusion that started suddenly, points at the nozzle or the feed: a partial clog, a worn nozzle, a slipping extruder. Ask the person to check those first.
- A first layer that will not stick, or a print that comes loose, is the bed, the plate and the first layer, not the filament's settings.

When none of the tests fits, say so instead of offering one.

## Before making a test

Say two things in your own words and get a reply before calling calibration_generate: the open project will be saved to its version history and closed, and the test opens as a project of its own; the test changes settings only for itself, and nothing is saved to a preset until the person chooses. End with a Choices line, such as "Choices: Make the test | Not now".

When the person's message already says they are fine with the project being saved and closed (a Calibrate… row in the app writes that for them, after showing both facts), they have answered: do not ask again. If they have not said which test, or what they are seeing, ask that instead, with the tests as choices.

## The three tests

Read the printer, the filament preset and its material from the workspace. Ranges below are mine, and calibration_generate refuses one outside what I accept.

**Temperature.** A tower of blocks, each printed 5 °C cooler than the one below it, labelled with its temperature. start is the bottom block's, the hottest; end the top's; both multiples of 5, start at least 5 hotter. My ranges by material: PLA 230 to 190; ABS and ASA 270 to 230; PETG 250 to 230; PCTG 280 to 240; TPU 240 to 210; PA-CF and PET-CF 320 to 280. Narrow one to the filament's own nozzle_temperature_range_low and nozzle_temperature_range_high when those are tighter (settings_get, filament scope). For another material, centre the range on the preset's nozzle_temperature.
Photograph: the side with the numbers, close enough to read them, in light from one side so strings and droops show. Reading: too hot strings, sags under the overhangs and bridges and looks glossy and blobby; too cold looks rough and dull, bridges poorly, and layers may split. The best block is the coolest one that still bonds and bridges cleanly. It writes nozzle_temperature, and nozzle_temperature_initial_layer kept at the same offset from it the preset had.

**Flow.** Tiles printed at different flow, each with its change embossed on it and in its object name. linear true, the default, is the recommended set, whose tiles add an amount to the flow ratio (-.05 to +.05 on pass 1, finer on pass 2); linear false is the classic set, whose tiles name a percentage change. Start with pass 1; offer pass 2 only when two neighbouring tiles look equally good.
Photograph: the top surfaces from straight above, in light from one side, all tiles in view. Reading: the best tile has a smooth, closed top with no gaps between lines and no ridges or a raised edge. Read filament_flow_ratio with settings_get first: the new value is that plus the tile's amount for the recommended set, or that times (100 + the tile's percentage) / 100 for the classic set. It writes filament_flow_ratio.

**Pressure advance.** method tower, the default, prints a tower whose pressure advance rises by step for each millimetre of height from start at the bottom; line prints numbered lines; pattern prints numbered corners. Leave start, end and step to calibration_generate's defaults unless the person asks; give extruderType bowden for a printer that feeds through a long tube, otherwise leave it. Bambu Lab printers measure this themselves before a print when flow dynamics calibration is on, and the value they measure stays on the printer: say so before offering the test on one.
Photograph: tower: the corners from the side, with a ruler beside it or the height where they look best; line or pattern: from straight above, numbers in view. Reading: the best height or line has sharp corners with no bulge before them and no gap or thin wall after them. For the tower the value is start plus the best height in millimetres times step; for line and pattern, the number by the best one. It writes pressure_advance, with enable_pressure_advance on.

All three write the filament preset.

## After making a test

The test's project opens with my note of what I made. In that turn, call setup_record with the test as the purpose (such as "Temperature test for Bambu PLA Basic") and the range as the headline, then slice it with slice_start. Tell the person to print it, what to photograph and how, and to send the photo here.

When the person comes back to a temperature or pressure-advance test, check its plate in the workspace: while the plate carries calibration, its steps are in place. Without it the test was saved and reopened, which keeps the tower but not its steps, so it would print at one setting: say so, and offer to make it again with the same range before anyone slices or prints it. A flow test keeps its tiles' ratios and needs nothing.

## Reading the photo and saving the result

Name the best block, tile or height and why, and the runner-up. If the photo cannot show it (blurry, too far, the wrong side), ask for another before guessing. Then propose one write: settings_preview_patch on the filament preset in use, with persistAs, then settings_apply_patch with what the preview showed.

Step 1 is committed as `53d0fc4f4a`, and step 2, the calibration skill, is committed as `bab11c8eb1`. The skill file is attached for you to read.

**What the skill tells the agent:**
- **When a test is worth it.** Stringing points to temperature first (retraction next, which has no test yet). Gaps or an over-full top point to flow. Bulging corners point to pressure advance. result.output:
### A system alert looked foreign next to OrcaSlicer's own questions

**Observed problem:** The "Previously opened file" question was a
`wxMessageDialog`, which on macOS is a system `NSAlert`: a narrow column with
the app icon above wrapped text and stacked buttons. Kenneth reviewed the
screenshots on 2026-10-14 and found it ugly next to every other question the
app asks. An earlier change had made the same mistake and fixed it the same
way (`ShellController::offer_agent_setup`, d0bce03db3). Other JusPrin
`wxMessageBox` and `wxMessageDialog` calls remain.

**Resolution:** The question uses OrcaSlicer's `MessageDialog` (`MsgDialog.hpp`),
with `SetButtonLabel` for its buttons. That dialog highlights Yes as the
primary button, so the suggested choice is put on Yes. Every `DPIAware`
dialog first passes through `answer_modal` (`DialogListeners.hpp`), and a
person's file open answers each one on its own. A dialog that asks the person
something during an open therefore needs a listener that returns
`kShowToPerson` for that one dialog.

**Lesson for future agents:** Ask the person through OrcaSlicer's
`MessageDialog`, never `wxMessageDialog` or `wxMessageBox`. Then check whether
the call can run while a file open or a tool call is answering dialogs, and if
it can, let that one dialog through on purpose. Review a new dialog from a
picture, not only from its text: the shell harness can draw a modal window to
a PNG with no screen permission (`snapshot_native_window`, used by
`--reopen-prompt`).

Add the Calibrate... rows: printer chip, filament slot and Home printer card

Three entry rows, as board 1 of the canvas's calibration page places them:
"Calibrate..." above "Printer settings..." in the project header's printer
menu, "Calibrate this filament..." above "Filament settings..." in the
filament slot menu, and "Calibrate..." after "Printer settings..." in a
saved printer's Home card menu. One row each, with no test named: the
assistant asks which test fits (Kenneth, 2026-10-21), so adding a test stays
a declaration and skill text.

Every row goes through ShellController::start_calibration. Without an
assistant it offers the assistant's setup. Otherwise OrcaSlicer's
MessageDialog says what board 3 says, the test named by the assistant
later: the open project is saved and closed when the test starts, and the
test's settings are temporary. Cancel changes nothing. Start test leaves
Home or the printer chat for the project chat and sends the request there
as the person's own message, saying what they agreed to ("Calibrate <filament>
on <printer>. I'm fine with <project> being saved and closed for the
test."), so the calibration skill does not ask again. The message goes
through submit_issue_message, the path for a person's words from a button
outside the page, with no issue context.

A Home card names its printer and no filament; the skill now tells the
assistant to set that printer up with printer_setup before making the test
(Kenneth's choice over the app switching it). Home's bridge gains
calibrate_printer, within protocol version 1 (the bridge has not shipped).
The Home menu has no separator style, so its row comes without the board's
line. offer_agent_setup takes the sentence to show.

The note a test's project opens its chat with now speaks as the app ("The
temperature tower is ready in this project..."), not of OrcaSlicer as
another program.

Tests: the shell harness gains --calibration-capture, with a stand-in
assistant and real clicks on the real rows: the filament row's and the Home
card's dialogs are cancelled and leave the project and the chat as they
were; the printer row's is accepted, the person's request arrives, the
assistant asks which test, the Temperature chip is tapped, and
calibration_generate opens the test's own project, whose chat opens with
the app's note and whose plate reports its steps. It writes a picture of
the window, menu or dialog at each step. The default run's filament-menu
row list includes the new row. jusprin_tests covers the Home route, HomeUI
the kebab row and its message, AgentUI the skill's new line.

Verified on Windows: --calibration-capture passes (21 checks) and its
pictures were looked at; jusprin_tests [home], HomeUI npm test (63/63),
the AgentUI skill tests and agent_bridge_tests pass apart from failures
that already occur on a Windows checkout. Not run on macOS.

---
name: native-ui-synthetic-input-and-capture
description: "Driving JusPrin's native (wx) UI on the Windows box with real pointer and key input from PowerShell, and capturing it — the four traps that each looked like an app bug"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 5f4606f5-f6a6-45fd-a91f-ea049831eb87
  modified: 2026-10-14T17:09:59.148Z
---

With the RDP session **connected** (see [[windows-ui-testing-without-a-desktop]] for the disconnected case), native wx surfaces can be driven from PowerShell with `SetCursorPos` + `mouse_event` + `keybd_event` and captured with `Graphics.CopyFromScreen`. Worked on 2026-10-02 for the left pane (`shell_integration_harness --manual-left-pane`). Four traps, each of which first looked like a defect in the app:

- **Arrow keys need `KEYEVENTF_EXTENDEDKEY` (flag 1).** Without it `keybd_event(VK_DOWN)` arrives as `WXK_NUMPAD_DOWN` (379), not `WXK_DOWN` (317), so a handler testing only `WXK_DOWN` looks dead. (Real numpad arrows send the same code, so handlers should accept both.)
- **The GL canvas takes keyboard focus when the pointer enters it.** Parking the cursor over the canvas between a click and a key press moves focus off the control under test. Park it inside the surface being tested.
- **Coordinates are virtualized, the screen copy is not.** PowerShell is DPI-unaware: `GetWindowRect`/`SetCursorPos` use logical units (screen reads 1728x1084 at 200%), while `CopyFromScreen` wants real pixels. Multiply by `GetDeviceCaps(DESKTOPHORZRES=118) / GetDeviceCaps(HORZRES=8)`.
- **Tab is not available for focus traversal**: OrcaSlicer binds it to switching Prepare/Preview, and `wxWindow::Navigate()` is a no-op in this wx build (`wxHAS_NATIVE_TAB_TRAVERSAL`). Fork surfaces must move focus themselves (the left pane does it in a `wxEVT_CHAR_HOOK` handler).

**Why:** each cost a rebuild-and-retry loop before the cause turned out to be the instrument, not the code. Same lesson as [[verify-the-basic-path-in-the-app]].

**How to apply:** start from a scratch `ui.ps1` with Click-At / Press-Key / Capture helpers built on the rules above; when a key "does nothing", log the key code in the handler before changing the handler.

Related harness facts from the same session:
- `workspace_adapter_integration_harness.exe` gets no runtime DLLs copied beside it; run it with `C:\b\<tree>\tests\shell\Release` on `PATH` or it exits `0xC0000135`.
- In the default shell-harness mode, `failed_autosave_is_visible`, `failed_autosave_has_plain_status_text`, `failed_autosave_blocks_project_release` and `earlier_model_version_available` fail on Windows on an unmodified build too: the test makes a directory read-only with POSIX permissions, which Windows ignores. Since the Check Print crash was fixed (2026-10-14, `20de313d92`) the default mode runs to the end on this box: 552 pass, 6 fail. The other two failures, `agent_panel_columns_tile_the_client_shrinking_to_1000_dip` and `growing_to_1400_dip`, also fail with the fix switched off, with identical geometry, so they predate it. The filament-menu keyboard checks (`down_selects_the_first_filament` etc.) failed in 1 of 4 runs of the same binary, and that run then stalled on an open setup guide. See [[windows-build-machine]].
- A baseline for "is this failure mine": copy `C:\src\JusPrin\build\tests\shell\Release\*` to a scratch dir and run that exe (copying avoids locking the shared build's exe).

3:**Status:** This guide explains how to add a tool to JusPrin. The three things it builds on are already implemented: the shared tool registry, the MCP server embedded in the app, and the stdio bridge (a small helper program that connects external AI clients to that server). Over MCP, the tools currently cover inspecting the workspace, reporting on a slice for review, and the settings workflow. The settings workflow works on the process preset, on one object, and on filament and printer presets. Later in this guide there is a [candidate catalog](#candidate-catalog): a list of tools we might build, worked out from the product's screens. It follows the implemented catalog record. Nothing in the candidate catalog exists unless the catalog record says it does.
75:A fixed, mechanical step of a workflow can be a tool. Examples are generating OrcaSlicer's calibration geometry and starting OrcaSlicer's slice action. Advice should stay a skill until there is a separately specified operation behind it that always behaves the same way.
93:A skill is a file on the Agent page, `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: frontmatter with its `name` and a `trigger`, a `description` or both, then the text the model gets. The page sends every skill once per connection with the `skills` bridge message. A skill with a trigger is the app's: when the event it names happens, the host adds it to the one request where the model first reads about the event, as the request's last item, and to no later request. A skill with a description is the model's: `skill_read` lists the described skills in its own description and returns one by name, and is offered only while at least one exists. One skill has a description: `calibration`, read when a print problem may come from the filament or its settings, when the person asks to calibrate, or in a calibration test's project; it carries the conversation of a calibration (when a test is worth it, the two facts said before the open project closes, per-test ranges and how to read the print, the naming rule for the saved preset), while `calibration_generate`'s description keeps only that tool's rules. Four skills have triggers, one file each:
450:This catalog lists the tools the finished product would have. It was worked out one product screen at a time from [Designing an AI-Piloted OrcaSlicer](orca-feature-discovery.md), and shaped by the rules under [tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape). Nothing in it is implemented unless the catalog record above says so. Every row still needs what this guide requires of any tool: the eval failure, the trace of its owner, and the test matrix. The number that matters is how many definitions load per turn, not the total. The total here is 36. All of them load on every turn until the measurements under [tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape) justify deferral. 299:- A caller may pass a filesystem path only to a tool that does three things: it validates the exact absolute path, it restricts what kind of file the path may be and where, and it documents whether it reads, creates, or overwrites. The candidate catalog has three such tools: `object_import_file`, `project_open`, and `export_file`. No read-only tool accepts a path. In-app clients keep using attachments, which need no path.
450:This catalog lists the tools the finished product would have. 498:| `project_open` | D | Exactly one of `path`, `new: true`, or `versionId`. Explicit inputs for the choices Orca otherwise asks in dialogs: `loadProjectSettings` (project or keep), `unitConversion` (none, inches to millimetres); every dialog Orca raises while loading is answered with the least change and returned in the load report. Replaces the document once the autosave hook has saved the open one; unsaved preset edits are then dropped. A file opened as a project before returns `opened_before` (the project, and whether the file changed) until `openedBefore` says `existing` or `new`. | `Plater` load_project and load_files; backup restore | 32 import warnings |
516:| `object_import` | M | In-app only. Add a model from a chat attachment id to a target plate, with the same dialog-choice inputs as `project_open`. Retires `import_model`. | `Plater` load_files | 32 warnings |
1207:Paths supplied by a caller stay tightly restricted. `project_open` and `object_import_file` accept absolute paths that can be read. `export_file` requires the expected extension, a parent directory that already exists, and an explicit `overwrite` flag to replace a file. It refuses OrcaSlicer's data directory and its temporary project directories. `project_attachment_read` accepts only an attachment ID, which it resolves inside the project attachment directory. These restrictions limit accidental damage. They do not replace authenticating local clients.
override. Only Undo, or the object settings panel, does.

### Registry facts worth knowing

- `ToolExecutionCoordinator::execute` dispatches on `ToolHandler`, with one
  explicit block of code per tool. Add a block for each new tool. Do not
  replace the blocks with a generic dispatch table.
- `kInvalidatingReasons` is the mask of change reasons that make most queued
  actions stale. It includes `Settings`, so a queued action fails with
  `stale_revision` when the user edits a setting in the GUI.
  `settings_apply_patch` has its own mask, `Settings | Project`. The reason
  is something the M5 live eval showed: an agent annotated a region between
  its settings preview and its apply, and that model edit (and the slicing
  events after it) made every apply stale. A settings patch is already bound
  to the "before" values it previewed, and the apply checks those values
  again. So its `expectedRevision` only has to be no older than the last
  settings or project change. Model edits do not matter.
- `ToolRegistry::validate_output` accepts only these schema keywords: `type`,
  `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, `items`, `minimum`,
  `maxItems`, `enum`, `maxLength`. Any other keyword throws. Before using a
  new keyword, extend the validator and add a test. `enum` is checked
  whatever the value's type. `maxLength` counts UTF-8 bytes, which matches
  the byte bounds this registry states everywhere else.

{"spools": [{"subBrands": "PLA Matte", "trayType": "PLA", "colour": "5F7D4FFF"}]}
```

`subBrands` is what `PrinterDiscovery.cpp` reads back as the spool's name
when set (ahead of `trayType`), so it is the field worth setting for a
saved/network-printer card or receipt to show something. `trayType` is the
spool's material (Home's Loaded row names it); the fake sends it beside a
`tray_info_idx`, since upstream ignores a type that arrives without one.
`filamentId` sets that id (`"GFA01"` is Bambu PLA Matte); left out, the
id is empty, and Orca's filament sync skips the tray. `colour` is optional: a spool without it reports no colour, and Home
draws no swatch for it.

Delete the file, or set `"offline": false` and `"state":"idle"`, to return to Idle.

## Print

Slice, then Print (or Cmd+Shift+G on macOS). Send completes without a printer.
The log records `FakeBambuAgent: start_local_print file=...`.

If the control file is present, that file wins: send still succeeds, but the
menu stays on the file's state. Remove the file if you want the canned printing
scenario after send.

## Isolate a running app (agents)

Another JusPrin may already be open. Do not send keys or clicks to it.

On macOS both processes are often named `OrcaSlicer`. Target by unix pid or by
a unique `CFBundleIdentifier` on a ditto'd `.app` (then ad-hoc `codesign`).
`osascript` `unix id` filters can match the wrong process; prefer
`AXUIElementCreateApplication(pid)` or the unique bundle id.

Keyboard events posted to the pid work while the Mac is locked; mouse events
posted that way do not. Menus only open when that app is frontmost. The printer
half of the chip is a wx control (`SetName("Printer")`) and often has no AX
title; click by coordinates after a screenshot, or use the documented shortcut
for Print.

Logs: `<datadir>/log/debug_*.log`. This machine's default `grep` may be ugrep;
use `/usr/bin/grep -a` on app logs.

## Unit tests

`jusprin_fake_bambu_tests` (Catch2, GUI build). They cover announce JSON,
control-file parsing, and agent id. They do not start the heartbeat unless the
test sets `set_queue_on_main_fn`.

## Agent id

Registered as `jusprin-fake-bambu`. `GUI_App::switch_printer_agent` uses that
id in place of `bbl` when fake mode is on. No other upstream file is involved.

using System;

  [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential)] public struct RECT { public int Left, Top, Right, Bottom; }

# The harness window through PrintWindow with PW_RENDERFULLCONTENT, which
# draws GL and WebView2 and works while the RDP session is disconnected
# (a screen copy is blank then). DPI-aware, so the rectangle is real pixels.
Add-Type -AssemblyName System.Drawing
Add-Type @"
using System;
using System.Runtime.InteropServices;
public static class Shot {
  [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential)] public struct RECT { public int Left, Top, Right, Bottom; }
  [DllImport("user32.dll")] public static extern bool GetWindowRect(IntPtr h, out RECT r);
  [DllImport("user32.dll")] public static extern bool PrintWindow(IntPtr h, IntPtr dc, uint flags);
  [DllImport("user32.dll")] public static extern bool SetProcessDPIAware();
}
"@
[Shot]::SetProcessDPIAware() | Out-Null
$id = (Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='shell_integration_harness.exe'" | Where-Object { $_.CommandLine -match $Match } | Select-Object -First 1).ProcessId
$h = (Get-Process -Id $id).MainWindowHandle
Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 1500
$r = New-Object Shot+RECT

$bmp = New-Object System.Drawing.Bitmap ($r.Right - $r.Left), ($r.Bottom - $r.Top)
$g = [System.Drawing.Graphics]::FromImage($bmp)
$dc = $g.GetHdc()
[Shot]::PrintWindow($h, $dc, 2) | Out-Null
$g.ReleaseHdc($dc)
$bmp.Save($Out, [System.Drawing.Imaging.ImageFormat]::Png)

2	name: windows-ui-testing-without-a-desktop
3	description: How to drive real JusPrin UI gestures on the Windows box when the RDP session is disconnected (SetCursorPos and screen capture both die; send WM_ messages and read geometry instead)
4	metadata:

11	When the RDP session to the Windows verification box is **disconnected** (`query session` shows state `Disc` for the `guitest` session), `SetCursorPos`/`mouse_event` silently do nothing — `GetCursorPos` keeps returning 0,0 — and `Graphics.CopyFromScreen` throws "The handle is invalid". Only a *connected* session has an input desktop.
12	
13	**Why:** This looks exactly like an application bug — gestures appear to have no effect and screenshots fail — so it can burn a long time before you realise the session, not the code, is the problem.
14	
15	**How to apply:**
16	- Check `query session` first when input or capture stops working.
17	- Real UI testing still works without a desktop: `SendMessageTimeout` WM_LBUTTONDOWN / WM_MOUSEMOVE / WM_LBUTTONUP / WM_LBUTTONDBLCLK straight to the child HWND. This goes through the real wxMSW window procedure, real `SetCapture`, and real double-click handling — strictly more real than the harness's `ProcessEvent` injection, which bypasses `MSWWindowProc` entirely.
18	- A faithful drag must hold the pointer at a fixed **screen** x and recompute the client x from the target window's live `GetWindowRect` each step. Holding client x fixed makes a moving splitter run away, because the app converts with `ClientToScreen` against the window's current position.
19	- Read results from `EnumChildWindows` + `GetWindowRect` rather than pixels; assert that sibling columns tile the client rect exactly, which catches overlaps a per-window size check cannot see.
20	- P/Invoke `GetWindowTextW` must be declared `CharSet=CharSet.Unicode`, or the StringBuilder is marshalled as ANSI and the W call overruns the buffer and crashes PowerShell.
21	- The harness holds `shell_integration_harness.exe` open; kill it before relinking or the link fails with LNK1104.
22	- See [[windows-build-machine]] for the Mesa/GL and toolchain facts.
